title: Gentle Giant Galaxy
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 289, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope
celestial: NGC 289 · constellation Sculptor · about 75 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), J. Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Bluish spiral arms reach across space in this view of NGC 289, a large, extended spiral galaxy in the constellation Sculptor. It lies around 75 million light-years away, yet its arms span more than 100,000 light-years, making it larger than our own Milky Way.

NGC 289 is classified as a Type II Seyfert galaxy, with rich patches of star formation and a bright core, but overall it is relatively faint. Studies have found that it holds large amounts of dark matter, a common trait of galaxies with low surface brightness. Surface brightness describes how much light a galaxy gives off for each patch of sky it covers, so faint, spread-out galaxies score low.

Dark matter has never been directly observed. Astronomers infer it from its gravitational pull on stars and gas. The image comes from the Dark Energy Camera (DECam), mounted on the Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile. The camera has been open to other scientists since its original survey ended.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (13.10 x 13.10 arcminutes) and distance (75 million light years), the frame spans roughly 286,000 × 286,000 light-years. Its light set out about 75 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Taken with DECam on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope through g, r and z filters. The color mapping isn't published.
